Patient demographics:
  age: 71
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Insurance Agent
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Stranger Interaction: Talking to strangers, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Prevention: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Vignette:
Elliot Thompson, a 71-year-old insurance agent, sat silently in the waiting room, the hum of fluorescent lights above him mingling with the murmur of distant voices. He had spent the last few weeks grappling with a persistent unease, an anxiety that felt like a specter haunting his everyday life. It was not the first time Elliot had been aware of this discomfort; it had been a steady companion since his childhood, but now it had grown too loud to ignore. 

Elliot’s trauma began in the dark corners of his childhood home, where his caregiver, someone he was supposed to trust, unleashed a torrent of physical abuse. Though the memories were hazy, the feelings associated with those moments remained vivid. When he thought about the abuse, Elliot could almost smell the stale alcohol on his caregiver's breath, a scent that surged up unbidden, wrapping around him like a shroud. It was this olfactory recall that would sometimes immobilize him as he sat alone in his modest apartment, the faintest whiff of alcohol on the street below causing his heart to race and his palms to sweat. 

In his current life, Elliot found himself avoiding situations that might trigger these memories. He dreaded talking to strangers, as even innocuous interactions could spiral into feelings of vulnerability and fear. Just last week, a passerby had asked him for directions, and Elliot had felt a surge of panic, the stranger's approach igniting a deep-seated sense of threat. He had hurried away, heart pounding, convinced that he was being targeted, even in what should have been a mundane exchange. These moments were becoming more frequent, leaving him feeling increasingly isolated. 

To cope with the constant sense of danger, Elliot had developed a series of mental rituals—small, magical acts that he hoped would stave off bad outcomes. He would count the steps from his living room to the kitchen, repeating a mantra in his head to keep the darkness at bay. If he could keep his mind occupied, he believed, he might prevent the worst from happening. Watching television or reading about similar events became a no-go zone; he found himself avoiding any media that might trigger those haunting memories or remind him of his past. The world outside his window had become a place filled with dangers, and he felt compelled to guard himself against them, even if it meant retreating into a solitary existence.

The intrusion monitoring became a way of life for him; he would often listen intently for sounds that might betray an unwanted presence in his home. Every creak of the floorboards or rustle of leaves outside sent him into a state of hyper-alertness. It was exhausting, yet he felt powerless to change his behavior. His body had betrayed him, reacting as though he were still in danger, even in the safety of his own living room. He often thought that he was living in a world where he was constantly on edge, a prisoner to the fears that had been instilled in him all those years ago.

As he recalled those memories, fragments would flash before him unexpectedly—faces, places, and sensations that felt more real than the mundane details of his everyday life. Elliot had come to believe that the people responsible for his suffering had never faced consequences, leaving him with a sense of betrayal that echoed through the years. He felt trapped by a body that reacted with a sense of peril when he was, in fact, safe. 

Finally, it was the mounting weight of these experiences that had led him to seek help. A friend had expressed concern about his isolation, prompting Elliot to reflect on his life. He feared what might happen if he continued down this path—would he become completely unable to engage with the world around him? He hoped that therapy might provide him with tools to reclaim his life, to understand his memories and fears without being consumed by them. In this moment, sitting in the waiting room, he felt a flicker of hope—a tentative belief that perhaps he could find a way to live without the shadows of his past looming over him.
